scenario_stem:

A major label has offered a three-year contract for 120,000 records per month of a new compilation album, the largest single order in the firm's history. Spinwell could keep batch production, adding night shifts at overtime cost, or invest $900,000 in a dedicated flow line pressing only that title at 15,000 records per day. scenario_stem:

The brands pay on a net-30 basis, which squeezes cash flow further. Lenders see larger, safer businesses as less risky

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Wexford Steel Co of financial economies of scale.
questions.model_answer: One benefit is cheaper borrowing [k]. Wexford would pay 7% interest rather than the 11% typical for smaller rivals, saving $100,000 a year on a $2.5 million loan [app]. A second benefit is funding expansion from outside savings [k]. Access to a $2.5 million loan lets Wexford buy the electric furnace and raise output from 4,000 to 6,500 tonnes without waiting years to save the cash from revenue [app].

knowledge_max_2: Larger firms borrow at lower interest rates
Cheaper, easier finance funds growth and investment
application_max_2: Reference to 7% vs 11%, saving $100,000 a year on $2.5 million
Reference to electric furnace / capacity lifted from 4,000 to 6,500 tonnes

questions.question_text: Explain two risks to Wexford Steel Co of borrowing $2.5 million at 7% interest.
questions.model_answer: One risk is the fixed interest cost [k]. Interest of $175,000 a year must be paid even in a downturn [app], so if steel orders fall, Wexford could struggle to cover payments and last year's $900,000 profit would shrink fast, raising the danger of insolvency [an]. A second risk is over-committing to one customer [k]. The 5-year supply deal depends on the extra 2,500 tonnes being sold [app], and if demand does not materialise, Wexford would be left paying for an underused furnace while still owing the bank $2.5 million [an].

knowledge_max_2: Interest must be paid regardless of trading conditions
Debt creates repayment/insolvency risk if revenue falls
application_max_2: Reference to $175,000 a year interest / $900,000 profit last year
Reference to 5-year supply deal / extra 2,500 tonnes / $2.5 million loan
analysis_max_2: Chain from fixed interest to pressure on profit to risk of insolvency in a downturn
Chain from reliance on one deal to underused capacity to cash strain while still owing the bank

questions.question_text: Do you think Wexford Steel Co should borrow the $2.5 million? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: On one hand, borrowing at 7% shows a clear financial economy of scale [k]. Paying $175,000 interest a year instead of $275,000 at the 11% rate rivals typically pay saves $100,000 a year, and the furnace lifts capacity from 4,000 to 6,500 tonnes under a 5-year supply deal [app]. That extra scale would spread fixed costs, such as the depot and management, over more tonnes, lowering average cost and helping Wexford win further building-sector contracts [an]. On the other hand, debt adds pressure [k]. Even at 7%, Wexford commits $175,000 a year for many years, and profit of $900,000 last year could evaporate if construction demand falls or the 5-year deal is renegotiated smaller [app]. Staying at 4,000 tonnes avoids any risk to the 84 staff and keeps Wexford flexible if orders drop [an]. Overall, I think Wexford should borrow the $2.5 million [eval]. The guaranteed 5-year supply deal secures the extra 2,500 tonnes of sales, and the four percentage point interest advantage saves $100,000 a year, making expansion decisively worthwhile for an established supplier [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Financial economies of scale: larger firms borrow at lower interest rates
Debt increases fixed financial commitments and risk
application_max_2: Reference to 7% vs 11%, $175,000 vs $275,000 interest, saving $100,000 a year
Reference to 5-year supply deal, 6,500 tonnes vs 4,000 tonnes, $900,000 profit, 84 staff
analysis_max_2: Chain from lower interest and extra scale to lower average cost to more competitiveness
Chain from fixed interest commitments to pressure on $900,000 profit to insolvency risk if demand falls
evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation on borrowing the $2.5 million
Weighs both options using stem figures ($100,000 saving vs fixed $175,000 interest risk)

scenario_stem:
Carrick Pharmaceuticals is a private limited company in Country X making generic painkillers. It employs 120 workers and produces 80,000 packs a year, earning revenue of $8.4 million and profit of $950,000. Late deliveries and missed orders have doubled since last year. Output has outgrown the office; general managers now cover marketing, production planning and finance at the same time.

Option A is to appoint three specialists, a marketing director, a production manager and a finance analyst, at a combined cost of $260,000 a year. They would aim to cut pack wastage from 9%, roughly $90,000 lost a year, to 3%. Option B is to keep the current generalist structure and postpone hiring until annual profit passes $1.1 million. The two owners disagree about the risk.

questions.question_text: Define 'managerial economies of scale'.
questions.model_answer: Managerial economies of scale are cost advantages where a larger business can afford specialist managers for particular functions, whose expertise reduces waste and improves decisions as the business grows [2].

knowledge_max_2: Large businesses can afford specialist managers
Specialist expertise reduces waste and improves decisions

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Carrick Pharmaceuticals of hiring specialist managers.
questions.model_answer: One benefit is better decisions in each function [k]. A dedicated marketing director, production manager and finance analyst would each give expert attention to their area instead of roles being covered by stretched generalists at a business employing 120 workers [app]. A second benefit is lower wastage [k]. Targeting wastage from 9% to 3% would cut roughly $60,000 of the $90,000 lost each year, protecting part of the $950,000 profit [app].

knowledge_max_2: Specialist managers make better decisions in their function
Specialists reduce waste and errors in the business
application_max_2: Reference to 120 workers / general managers covering marketing, production planning and finance
Reference to wastage cut from 9% to 3% / $90,000 lost a year / $950,000 profit

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Carrick Pharmaceuticals might face from hiring the three specialists.
questions.model_answer: One problem is the salary cost [k]. The three specialists cost $260,000 a year, which would cut profit from $950,000 to roughly $690,000 before any savings are made [app]. If wastage does not fall as planned, Carrick would carry the extra payroll with no financial benefit in return [an]. A second problem is duplicated authority [k]. Adding a production manager above existing supervisors could create conflict over who makes decisions [app], and slow early coordination between new and existing managers could delay the very efficiency gains the hires are meant to deliver [an].

knowledge_max_2: Senior specialists are expensive and reduce short-term profit
New managers can create conflict or duplication of authority
application_max_2: Reference to $260,000 combined annual salaries / profit $950,000 to about $690,000
Reference to a production manager above existing supervisors / current generalist structure
analysis_max_2: Chain from $260,000 salary cost to lower profit to pressure if savings do not materialise
Chain from overlapping authority to conflict or slow coordination to delayed efficiency gains

questions.question_text: Do you think Carrick Pharmaceuticals should hire the three specialists now? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: On one hand, managerial economies of scale apply as Carrick grows [k]. At 120 workers producing 80,000 packs a year, general managers are stretched across marketing, production planning and finance; specialists could cut wastage from 9% to 3%, saving about $60,000 a year of the $90,000 now lost [app]. Expert coordination would also reduce late deliveries and missed orders, protecting the $8.4 million revenue and supporting further efficient growth [an]. On the other hand, the cost is heavy [k]. Paying $260,000 a year would drop profit from $950,000 to about $690,000, and the two owners disagree; if savings fall short, waiting until annual profit passes $1.1 million, as Option B suggests, would be the safer route [app]. Duplicated authority and slow decisions between new and existing managers are also possible at this size [an]. Overall, I think Carrick should hire the three specialists now [eval]. The wastage saving plus better marketing and financial control make $260,000 good value against a $950,000 profit, and postponing to $1.1 million simply lets more waste accumulate [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Managerial economies of scale: specialists improve decisions and reduce waste as firms grow
Hiring costs reduce short-term profit and carries integration risks
application_max_2: Reference to 120 workers, 80,000 packs, wastage cut from 9% to 3%, about $60,000 of the $90,000 saved
Reference to $260,000 salaries, profit $950,000 to about $690,000, Option B threshold of $1.1 million, $8.4 million revenue

scenario_stem:
Silverline Electronics is a private limited company in Country X assembling home circuit-breaker panels. It employs 30 workers on manual assembly at $11 an hour, working 40 hours a week, producing 6,000 units a month; manual labour costs about $13,200 a week. Revenue last year was $5.6 million and profit was $700,000. Demand now exceeds capacity. Chloe Navarro, the managing director, believes the line would pay for itself through lower labour cost per unit, while the production manager fears defects during installation.

Option A is to buy an automated assembly line costing $1.8 million, run it with 8 operators, and raise output to 14,000 units a month. Option B is to stay with manual assembly, hire 12 extra workers at $11 an hour, and raise output to 8,500 units a month. The directors want the decision within 6 weeks.

questions.question_text: Define 'technical economies of scale'.
questions.model_answer: Technical economies of scale are cost advantages where a large business can afford advanced machinery and production techniques that lower the average cost per unit as output rises [2].

knowledge_max_2: Large businesses can afford advanced/automated machinery
Specialist techniques lower average cost per unit as output rises

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Silverline Electronics of buying the automated assembly line.
questions.model_answer: One benefit is higher output from fewer workers [k]. The line runs with 8 operators instead of 30 workers on manual assembly, lifting output from 6,000 to 14,000 units a month [app]. A second benefit is lower labour cost per unit [k]. Labour would fall from about $13,200 a week to about $3,520 a week, so the labour cost of each circuit-breaker panel would drop sharply as volume rises [app].

knowledge_max_2: Automated machinery raises output with fewer workers
Labour cost per unit falls as volume rises
application_max_2: Reference to 8 operators vs 30 workers / output 6,000 to 14,000 units a month
Reference to $13,200 a week labour vs about $3,520 a week / $11 an hour

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Silverline Electronics might face if it buys the automated assembly line.
questions.model_answer: One problem is the purchase price [k]. Paying $1.8 million would consume a large share of cash and is more than twice last year's $700,000 profit, so Silverline would likely need a loan or director funding [app]. If faults appear during installation, Silverline could pay interest while producing nothing, threatening profit [an]. A second problem is training and reliability [k]. The 8 operators must learn new controls, and a breakdown would halt production of up to 14,000 units a month [app], so one technical failure could cost far more than manual assembly ever would [an].

knowledge_max_2: Advanced machinery is expensive and strains cash flow
Automation brings training needs and breakdown risk
application_max_2: Reference to $1.8 million cost vs $700,000 profit last year
Reference to 8 operators needing training / 14,000 units a month at risk
analysis_max_2: Chain from $1.8 million spend to reliance on borrowing to profit pressure if installation fails
Chain from breakdown or poor training to halted production to heavy cost of failure

questions.question_text: Do you think Silverline Electronics should buy the automated assembly line? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: On one hand, technical economies of scale strongly favour the purchase [k]. The $1.8 million line raises output from 6,000 to 14,000 units a month, more than double, while manual labour falls from 30 workers to 8 operators [app]. Spreading fixed costs, such as factory rent and management, over more units lowers average cost per unit, and demand already exceeds capacity, so the extra panels can be sold without deep discounting [an]. On the other hand, the price tag is heavy [k]. At $1.8 million, the line is more than twice last year's $700,000 profit and would probably need borrowed money or director funding [app]. Option B, hiring 12 extra workers at $11 an hour to reach 8,500 units a month, is cheaper now, keeps flexibility and avoids installation defects that the production manager fears [an]. Overall, I think Silverline should buy the automated assembly line [eval]. Demand exceeds capacity and technical economies scale so well that the extra output of 5,500 units a month over Option B would quickly justify the $1.8 million, while Option B cannot match the fall in average cost per unit [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Technical economies of scale: automation lowers average cost per unit as output rises
Automation requires heavy upfront investment and carries installation risk
application_max_2: Reference to $1.8 million line, output 6,000 to 14,000 units, 30 workers to 8 operators
Reference to $700,000 profit, Option B of 12 extra workers at $11 an hour for 8,500 units
analysis_max_2: Chain from automation to spread fixed costs over more units to lower average cost per unit
Chain from $1.8 million upfront cost to financing risk to possible harm if installation fails
evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation on buying the automated line
Weighs both options using stem figures (14,000 vs 8,500 units; $1.8 million vs $700,000 profit)

scenario_stem:
The Meadowlark Dairy Co-operative in Country X is owned by 60 member farms. It collects and processes 150,000 litres of milk a day and employs 55 staff; the co-operative pays members $0.42 per litre collected. Last year revenue was $9.8 million and the surplus paid to members was $640,000. The board is weighing how to scale up processing capacity.

Option A is to build a new central plant costing $4 million, cutting average cost from $0.58 to $0.49 per litre and lifting capacity to 240,000 litres a day. Option B is to upgrade the existing line for $1.2 million, raising capacity to 190,000 litres a day. Members are split on whether a bigger plant risks paying farmers late; some fear coordination problems and slow decisions across a doubled site.

questions.question_text: Define 'scale of production'.
questions.model_answer: Scale of production is the size of a business's output, meaning how large the operation is and the volume of goods or services it produces [2].

knowledge_max_2: Scale of production refers to the size of output / the volume produced
It shows how large the business operation is

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Meadowlark of increasing its scale of production.
questions.model_answer: One benefit is lower average cost [k]. A new central plant would cut average cost from $0.58 to $0.49 per litre, saving 9 cents on every one of 240,000 litres processed each day [app]. A second benefit is greater capacity for member farms [k]. Capacity rising from 150,000 to 240,000 litres a day means all 60 member farms can sell more milk through the co-operative instead of seeking outside buyers [app].

knowledge_max_2: Larger scale can reduce average cost per unit
Larger scale gives more capacity and output
application_max_2: Reference to average cost $0.58 to $0.49 per litre / 9 cents saved
Reference to capacity 150,000 to 240,000 litres a day / 60 member farms

questions.question_text: Explain two diseconomies of scale Meadowlark might face at a large central plant.
questions.model_answer: One diseconomy is poor communication [k]. A bigger site with more drivers, engineers and member farms means messages travel further, and a quality problem in one shift could reach the board days late [app]. Slow reaction would waste more milk than the current 150,000-litres-a-day operation, hitting the $9.8 million revenue [an]. A second diseconomy is slow decision-making [k]. More layers of approval at a plant nearly twice the size mean routine decisions, such as buying parts or changing shifts, take longer [app], so the co-operative becomes sluggish just as larger rivals cut their prices [an].

knowledge_max_2: Poor communication as organisations grow larger
Slow decision-making as more layers of management are added
application_max_2: Reference to doubled/larger site vs current 150,000 litres a day / $9.8 million revenue
Reference to central plant / 60 member farms / more layers of approval
analysis_max_2: Chain from longer message routes to delayed response to wasted milk and lost revenue
Chain from more approval layers to slower decisions to sluggish response to rivals' price cuts

questions.question_text: Do you think Meadowlark Dairy Co-operative should build the large central plant? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: On one hand, bigger scale brings real economies [k]. The $4 million plant lifts capacity from 150,000 to 240,000 litres a day and cuts average cost from $0.58 to $0.49 per litre; on 240,000 litres a day, that 9-cent saving is about $21,600 a day [app]. Purchasing power for packaging, fuel and milk-collection logistics would also improve, supporting the $9.8 million revenue and the $640,000 surplus paid to members [an]. On the other hand, co-operatives fail when members feel ignored [k]. A plant 60% larger could bring poor communication and slower decisions across 60 farms, and if 240,000 litres cannot be sold profitably, member milk could be paid late, as some members fear [app]. Option B, upgrading the existing line for $1.2 million to reach 190,000 litres a day, is a cheaper and safer step that still adds capacity and avoids a doubled site [an]. Overall, I think Meadowlark should build the central plant [eval]. The $0.49 average cost and an extra 90,000 litres of daily capacity offer savings far beyond the $1.2 million upgrade, provided the board appoints extra supervisors to keep communication clear [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Larger scale of production can deliver economies of scale and lower average cost
Diseconomies of scale: poor communication and slow decision-making in large organisations
application_max_2: Reference to $4 million plant, $0.58 to $0.49 per litre, capacity 150,000 to 240,000 litres a day
Reference to $1.2 million upgrade to 190,000 litres, $9.8 million revenue, $640,000 surplus, 60 member farms
analysis_max_2: Chain from lower average cost and scale to better member surplus and competitiveness
Chain from larger, doubled site to coordination problems to risk of late payment to members
evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation on building the central plant
Weighs both options using stem figures ($21,600 a day saving vs $1.2 million cheaper upgrade)

scenario_stem:
Quickhaul Courier Services is a private limited company in Country X delivering parcels for online retailers. It has grown from 40 employees 18 months ago to 210 today, handling 15,000 parcels a day, with revenue of $6.3 million last year. Late deliveries have risen from 5% to 12% and two major clients have complained. Drivers report that messages from head office arrive too late to act on, and meeting notes are lost between depots.

Option A is to sign a national contract worth $1.4 million a year, pushing the workforce to about 400. Option B is to split Quickhaul into 3 regional divisions of around 70 staff, each with its own operations manager. The founder, Jess Marino, must decide before the contract signing deadline in 6 weeks.

questions.question_text: Identify two diseconomies of scale.
questions.model_answer: Poor communication, such as instructions from head office arriving late or being lost between depots [1]; slow decision-making, as more layers of management delay each approval [1].

knowledge_max_2: Poor communication as the business grows larger
Slow decision-making as more management layers are added

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Quickhaul Courier Services of splitting into regional divisions.
questions.model_answer: One benefit is better communication [k]. Divisions of around 70 staff would have shorter chains of command, so messages between depots and drivers would arrive on time and fewer parcels would be missed [app]. A second benefit is faster decision-making [k]. Each division's operations manager could approve routes and shifts without waiting for head office, helping to cut the 12% late-delivery rate back toward 5% [app].

knowledge_max_2: Smaller divisions shorten communication channels
Delegated decisions are made faster at division level
application_max_2: Reference to divisions of around 70 staff / lost messages between depots
Reference to 12% late deliveries vs 5% / operations manager per division

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Quickhaul Courier Services of signing the national contract.
questions.model_answer: One benefit is secure revenue [k]. The national contract is worth $1.4 million a year, giving Quickhaul predictable income on top of its current $6.3 million revenue [app]. Guaranteed volume would spread fixed costs, such as vehicles and depots, over more parcels a day, lowering average cost per delivery [an]. A second benefit is stronger market position [k]. With about 400 staff and 15,000-plus parcels a day, Quickhaul could win more online-retail contracts from rival couriers [app], and greater scale could unlock purchasing economies when buying fuel, tyres and packaging [an].

knowledge_max_2: A large contract secures predictable revenue
Greater scale spreads fixed costs and unlocks purchasing economies
application_max_2: Reference to $1.4 million a year contract / $6.3 million revenue
Reference to about 400 staff / 15,000 parcels a day
analysis_max_2: Chain from guaranteed volume to spread fixed costs to lower average cost per delivery
Chain from national scale to purchasing economies and stronger negotiating position

questions.question_text: Do you think Quickhaul Courier Services should sign the national contract worth $1.4 million a year? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: On one hand, signing the contract secures $1.4 million of annual revenue [k]. It would push the workforce from 210 to about 400 and lock in a large online retailer, helping Quickhaul spread fixed costs over 15,000-plus parcels a day and benefit from purchasing economies on fuel and vehicle parts [app]. This scale could secure Quickhaul's position as a national courier and lift profit above its current level [an]. On the other hand, growing to about 400 staff risks serious diseconomies of scale [k]. Deliveries are already 12% late, up from 5%, and drivers say head-office messages arrive too late; expanding to near double today's 210 as one organisation would likely worsen communication further [app]. Splitting into 3 regional divisions of around 70 staff, each with its own operations manager, would shorten chains of command and speed up decisions before capacity is stretched [an]. Overall, I think Quickhaul should sign the national contract only after splitting into regional divisions [eval]. The $1.4 million revenue is too valuable to refuse, but the rise from 5% to 12% late shows the current structure is already failing; divisions protect service quality while keeping the contract's scale [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Large contracts secure revenue and scale economies (purchasing, fixed cost spreading)
Diseconomies of scale: poor communication and slow decisions as firms grow
application_max_2: Reference to $1.4 million a year contract, workforce 210 to about 400, 15,000 parcels a day
Reference to deliveries 5% to 12% late, 3 regional divisions of around 70 staff
analysis_max_2: Chain from contract volume to fixed costs spread over more parcels to lower average cost and higher profit
Chain from larger single organisation to worse communication to rising late deliveries
evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation combining or choosing between the options

scenario_stem:
Driftwood Timber Co is a private limited company in Country X turning pine logs into fence panels. It employs 64 workers and produced 120,000 panels last year, with revenue of $1.92 million and a profit of $210,000. Total production costs were $1.71 million, equal to an average cost of $14.25 per panel. Driftwood's customers are two national builders' merchants who want 30% more panels next year.

Option A is to invest $350,000 in a larger kiln and an automated panel conveyor, lifting output to 200,000 panels a year and cutting waste from 12% of timber to 5%; the bank will lend at 8%. Option B is to keep current methods and repair the existing kiln for $40,000. The owner, Ruth Ellison, worries a bigger works may strain supervision.

questions.question_text: Define 'efficiency'.
questions.model_answer: Efficiency is producing the maximum possible output from a given amount of inputs, or minimising waste of time, materials and money in the production process [2].

knowledge_max_2: Efficiency means maximum output from given inputs
Efficiency means minimising waste of resources

questions.question_text: Explain two ways Driftwood Timber Co could improve its efficiency.
questions.model_answer: One way is investing in a larger kiln and conveyor [k]. Automating the movement of panels would lift output from 120,000 to 200,000 panels a year using the same 64 workers [app]. A second way is cutting timber waste [k]. Reducing waste from 12% to 5% of timber would get far more panels from each log, so the same raw materials would produce more saleable output [app].

knowledge_max_2: Automation can raise output from the same inputs
Reducing waste increases usable output from the same materials
application_max_2: Reference to output lifted from 120,000 to 200,000 panels / 64 workers unchanged
Reference to waste cut from 12% to 5% of timber

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Driftwood Timber Co might face if it expands to 200,000 panels a year.
questions.model_answer: One problem is higher supervisory strain [k]. A works operating at two-thirds more output needs tighter supervision, and without it the quality of fence panels could fall [app]. Defects found by the two national builders' merchants would damage Driftwood's reputation and future orders [an]. A second problem is larger fixed costs [k]. The $350,000 kiln and conveyor add to overheads at a works that currently earns $210,000 profit, and if demand from builders' merchants falls short of target, the extra capacity would be underused [app], leaving high fixed costs spread over fewer panels and raising average cost instead of lowering it [an].

knowledge_max_2: Rapid growth strains supervision and can reduce quality
Extra capacity raises fixed costs, which must be justified by demand
application_max_2: Reference to two national builders' merchants / output rose 120,000 to 200,000 panels
analysis_max_2: Chain from weaker supervision to defects to damaged reputation and lost orders
Chain from extra capacity to underused fixed costs to rising average cost if demand disappoints

questions.question_text: Do you think Driftwood Timber Co should invest $350,000 in the kiln and conveyor? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: On one hand, the investment lifts efficiency at a bigger scale [k]. Output would rise from 120,000 to 200,000 panels a year and waste would fall from 12% to 5%, so far more usable timber comes from each log and the average cost of $14.25 per panel should fall [app]. Technical economies like this lower average cost as output rises, and the bank would lend at 8% under Option A, so the extra capacity can be financed affordably [an]. On the other hand, expansion carries real risk [k]. Driftwood earned only $210,000 profit on revenue of $1.92 million, so $350,000 is about 1.7 times last year's profit [app]. If the two national builders' merchants do not take the extra 30% of panels, fixed costs would be spread over too few panels, profit would fall and the loan would be hard to repay [an]. Overall, I think Driftwood should invest the $350,000 [eval]. The 12% to 5% waste saving and automated output gain are decisive for a business facing a 30% demand increase, and the 8% bank loan is affordable; Option B only delays an inevitable decision [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Technical economies of scale lower average cost as output rises
Large investments raise fixed costs and financing risk
application_max_2: Reference to 120,000 to 200,000 panels, waste 12% to 5%, average cost $14.25, bank lends at 8%
Reference to $350,000 vs $210,000 profit, $1.92 million revenue, 30% more panels wanted by two builders' merchants
analysis_max_2: Chain from waste reduction and automation to lower average cost to higher profit
Chain from underused capacity to fixed costs spread over fewer panels to falling profit and loan pressure
evaluation_max_2: Makes a clear, justified recommendation on the $350,000 investment
Weighs both options using stem figures (waste 12% to 5% vs $350,000 cost and 30% demand rise)

scenario_stem:
Saltmarsh Chemicals Ltd is a private limited company in Country X producing industrial cleaning granules. It employs 150 workers and last year output was 220,000 kg, with revenue of $1.9 million, total costs of $1.32 million and a profit of $580,000. The present average cost is $6.00 per kg (total cost $1.32 million divided by 220,000 kg), and managers already report slow decisions between the two halls.

Option A is to spend $2.2 million on a third production hall to lift output to 330,000 kg a year, projecting average cost near $5.10 per kg. Option B is to keep two halls, keep output at 220,000 kg and protect the $580,000 profit. Bank lending for Option A would run for 8 years at 6%.

questions.question_text: Calculate the average cost per kg last year when total costs were $1.32 million and output was 220,000 kg.
questions.model_answer: Average cost = total cost / output = $1,320,000 / 220,000 kg = $6.00 per kg [2].

Lifting output from 220,000 to 330,000 kg a year would spread fixed costs over 50% more units, projecting average cost near $5.10 per kg instead of $6.00 [app]. A second benefit is greater capacity to accept orders [k]. A third hall would let Saltmarsh take on larger contracts from industrial customers without turning work away to rival suppliers [app].

With three halls, approvals for maintenance, shifts and purchases would pass through more managers, so routine decisions take longer [app]. That could delay urgent repairs and cut availability of the halls below plan [an]. A second diseconomy is poor communication [k]. A workforce expanding beyond 150 workers would need clearer reporting lines [app], and without them mistakes in handling industrial cleaning granules could cause accidents or rejected batches [an].

knowledge_max_2: Slow decision-making as more management layers are added
Poor communication as the workforce grows larger
application_max_2: Reference to three halls / more managers for decisions

questions.question_text: Do you think Saltmarsh Chemicals Ltd should build the third production hall? Justify your answer.

Benefit 2: it helps decide whether the $26,000 cold-room purchase in August is affordable [k]; the July closing balance will be about $6,450 (opening $2,600 plus net cash flow of +$3,850), far below the purchase price, so the forecast tells her extra finance or a postponement is essential [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: A cash-flow forecast highlights periods of expected shortage or surplus in advance
It supports decisions about large or irregular purchases
application_max_2: Applies the June deficit of $1,800 and the 60 debtors as early-warning use

analysis_max_2: Explains that early warning allows action before the shortfall hits

questions.question_text: Do you think Jenny should buy the cold room now using an overdraft, or postpone it by six months? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Jenny could argue the cold room should be bought now so it is ready for the August vegetable peak [k]. However, the forecast shows only $2,600 opening in July and a +$3,850 net cash flow, so a $26,000 payment would swallow all available cash and push the shop deeper into overdraft while June is already forecast at -$1,800 [app][an]. Postponing six months protects the thin position and lets the shop build its balance from the stronger July forecast of $12,750 inflows, though it delays the extra capacity a growing shop with 210 customers may need [app][an]. Because postponement is reversible and cheap, whereas an overdraft is not guaranteed [k][eval], the sensible decision is to postpone the cold room until autumn sales are banked and only then confirm the purchase [eval].

scenario_stem:
Bluewater Surf School is a sole trader business run by Kai Delgado on the coast of Country X, teaching surf lessons to about 480 pupils each April-to-September season. Kai employs 4 instructors. His forecast shows July inflows of $18,600 against outflows of $13,400, August inflows of $15,200 against outflows of $14,750, and September inflows of only $6,800 against outflows of $9,900. He begins September with an opening balance of $7,900.

The school has current assets of $22,000 and current liabilities of $14,500, leaving working capital of $7,500. Kai wants to buy two new rescue boards costing $3,400 each in October, but the quiet winter months worry him. He is considering delaying the purchase until the spring term or taking out a small bank overdraft to cover the off-season shortfall.

questions.question_text: Define 'opening balance'.
questions.model_answer: Opening balance is the cash a business has available at the start of a period, brought forward from the previous period's closing balance (Bluewater Surf School begins September with $7,900). [2]

knowledge_max_2: Opening balance is the cash held at the start of a period
The opening balance equals the previous closing balance

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why September is the hardest month of the season for Bluewater Surf School's cash flow.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: demand collapses once the season ends [k]; the forecast shows September inflows of only $6,800 against $18,600 in July and $15,200 in August [app]. Reason 2: outflows are slower to fall than inflows [k]; September outflows of $9,900 still exceed inflows, giving a net cash flow of -$3,100 and leaving a September closing balance of only $4,800 [app].

Fixed-style outflows (wages, storage) continue when revenue falls

Applies September outflows of $9,900 vs inflows of $6,800, i.e. -$3,100 and closing $4,800

questions.question_text: Explain two ways Kai could overcome the cash-flow problem he expects in September.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Kai could ask his bank for an overdraft [k]; this covers the September shortfall of $3,100 so the school keeps paying instructors and boat maintenance while it waits for next season's deposits [app][an]. Way 2: he could delay buying the two new rescue boards costing $3,400 each until spring [k]; postponing this $6,800 capital item protects the $7,500 working capital and keeps September liquid [app][an].

Delaying or cancelling capital expenditure reduces cash outflow

Applies the $3,400 boards x 2 = $6,800 against the $7,500 working capital
analysis_max_2: Explains that an overdraft bridges the gap until next season's income arrives
Explains that delaying a discretionary purchase is a cheaper way to protect cash

questions.question_text: Do you think Kai should buy the two rescue boards in October, or delay until the spring term? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Kai could argue the boards should be bought now, before the winter, because they are essential safety equipment for a school teaching 480 pupils and because October prices may rise [k]. scenario_stem:
Redbank Construction Ltd is a private limited company founded 9 years ago by Marta Okoro in Country X, employing 38 staff across two housing sites and a small joinery workshop. March inflows are forecast at $21,500 against outflows of $29,300.

Redbank begins April with an opening balance of $5,100 and forecasts April inflows of $27,800 against outflows of $22,400. Marta is considering offering the housing association a 2% early-payment discount to bring the $34,000 in sooner, taking a $20,000 bank loan, or delaying the $32,000 cement mixer order until the association pays. She must decide before the April payroll.

questions.question_text: Define 'closing balance'.
questions.model_answer: Closing balance is the cash a business has at the end of a period, found by adding the net cash flow to the opening balance (Redbank begins April with $5,100 and April's forecast net cash flow is +$5,400, giving a closing balance of $10,500). [2]

knowledge_max_2: Closing balance is the cash remaining at the end of a period
Closing balance = opening balance + net cash flow

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Redbank Construction of offering the 2% early-payment discount to the housing association.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: the discount should pull cash in sooner [k]; the housing association is 60 days late and owes $34,000, so pulling even half into April would more than cover the $22,400 of April outflows [app]. Benefit 2: a 2% discount is cheap finance [k]; giving up $680 on $34,000 costs far less than the interest on a $20,000 bank loan and still lands before the April payroll [app].

knowledge_max_2: An early-payment discount encourages debtors to pay faster, improving cash flow
A small discount can be cheaper than interest on borrowed finance
application_max_2: Applies the $34,000 owed and 60 days late payment by the housing association
Applies 2% of $34,000 = $680 against the $22,400 April outflows and $20,000 loan

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why delaying the $32,000 cement mixer order could help Redbank's cash flow.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: delaying postpones a very large capital outflow [k]; moving the $32,000 mixer out of April keeps April outflows at $22,400 and lets the forecast opening balance of $5,100 recover to about $10,500 without new borrowing [app][an]. Reason 2: it avoids committing before the association pays [k]; with the client 60 days late on $34,000, delaying the purchase means Redbank is not forced into a $20,000 loan before knowing when cash will actually arrive [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Delaying or cancelling capital expenditure is a remedy for a short-term cash-flow problem
Avoiding new long-term borrowing reduces interest costs and insolvency risk
application_max_2: Applies the $32,000 mixer vs April outflows of $22,400 and opening balance of $5,100
Applies the association's 60-day lateness and the $34,000 owed to the loan alternative
analysis_max_2: Explains that delaying pushes the large outflow beyond the strained month
Explains that commitment before payment risks inability to fund the April payroll

questions.question_text: Do you think Marta should offer the early-payment discount, or take the $20,000 bank loan? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Marta could argue for the 2% early-payment discount because it tackles the root problem [k]. Costing only $680 on $34,000, it is cheaper than a $20,000 loan, avoids new debt and matches the fact that the housing association is already 60 days late [app][an]. However, the discount only helps if the association agrees and pays promptly, so if it still pays slowly the April payroll remains at risk and a loan - or the mixer delay - may still be needed [app][an]. Because the discount is cheap and non-binding while the mixer delay alone does not guarantee cash [k][eval], the evidence favours offering the discount first and taking the $20,000 loan only if the association refuses [eval]; the decision should be made before the April payroll, not after it.

scenario_stem:
Saffron Spice Restaurant is an independent curry house in Country X opened 6 years ago by brothers Dev and Priya Nair, serving about 95 covers on a busy Saturday and 40 covers on weekdays, with both brothers working the stoves six nights a week. It rents rather than owns its kitchen equipment and turns over $38,000 a month. Current assets are $15,600 and current liabilities are $19,200.

After a roof leak in February, the Nairs face an unexpected $7,400 repair bill. The February forecast shows inflows of $31,800 against outflows of $34,600, while March forecasts $36,500 inflows against $33,100 outflows. They are deciding between a $9,000 bank overdraft and asking the spice wholesaler for a further 45 days credit before paying their February bill.

questions.question_text: Define 'overdraft'.
questions.model_answer: An overdraft is a short-term bank facility allowing a business to withdraw more money than it holds in its account, up to an agreed limit, with interest charged on the amount borrowed. [2]

knowledge_max_2: An overdraft is a short-term bank facility to spend more than the balance
Interest is charged only on the amount overdrawn

questions.question_text: Explain two problems caused by the restaurant's negative working capital position.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: current liabilities exceed current assets [k]; the restaurant holds only $15,600 of current assets against $19,200 of short-term debts, so working capital is negative at -$3,600 [app]. Problem 2: the business runs a cash deficit before the repair bill is paid [k]; February outflows of $34,600 already exceed inflows of $31,800, so the February net cash flow of -$2,800 plus the $7,400 roof bill means new finance is needed [app].

knowledge_max_2: Working capital = current assets - current liabilities; negative means short-term debts exceed short-term assets
Negative working capital risks inability to pay debts as they fall due
application_max_2: Applies $15,600 vs $19,200 giving working capital of -$3,600
Applies February inflows of $31,800 and outflows of $34,600 (-$2,800) plus the $7,400 repair

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of the $9,000 overdraft compared with asking the spice wholesaler for 45 days credit.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: the overdraft lets the repair proceed immediately without starving the kitchen [k]; the February gap of -$2,800 and the $7,400 bill mean a $9,000 facility covers both [app][an]. Benefit 2: it keeps the supplier relationship intact [k]; asking the spice wholesaler for 45 days credit risks delayed or refused spice deliveries exactly when the March forecast of $36,500 inflows depends on full service, while March outflows of $33,100 still fall due [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: An overdraft is flexible short-term finance matched to the cash gap
Delaying supplier payments can damage the supplier relationship and supply of goods
application_max_2: Applies the -$2,800 February gap and the $7,400 repair vs the $9,000 overdraft
Applies March inflows of $36,500 and outflows of $33,100 to the delivery risk
analysis_max_2: Explains the overdraft covers both the deficit and the repair bill without affecting suppliers
Explains refused credit could disrupt supply in the strongest trading month

questions.question_text: Do you think the Nairs should take the $9,000 overdraft, or ask the spice wholesaler for 45 days credit? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The Nairs could argue for the overdraft because it keeps the wholesaler relationship safe while fixing the roof immediately [k]. A $9,000 facility would cover the -$2,800 February deficit and the $7,400 repair, and interest is paid only on what is drawn [app][an]. However, an overdraft is repayable on demand and adds a fixed monthly cost, so if March disappoints below the $36,500 inflow forecast the bank could call the facility in [app][an]. Because the wholesaler credit would cost nothing if granted but risks refusal and reputational damage [k][eval], the evidence favours taking the $9,000 overdraft now, agreed in writing, while honouring the March payment to the wholesaler in full [eval]; the decision should be reversed only if the bank refuses or prices the facility punitively.

knowledge_max_2: An overdraft provides immediate short-term finance but is repayable on demand
Asking suppliers for more credit is free but damages the business relationship

Applies the March forecast of $36,500 inflows / $33,100 outflows to the overdraft risk
analysis_max_2: Explains the overdraft covers both the deficit and the repair without touching the supplier
Explains that a call-in risk exists if March underperforms

scenario_stem:
Larkspur Florist is a partnership owned by Emma and Lucy Hartley in Country X, selling fresh flowers, wedding arrangements and weekly office subscriptions. It forecasts May inflows of $8,700 including $1,900 from two weddings against outflows of $10,300, and June inflows of $9,800 against outflows of $8,150; it also sells wedding corsages all year round. It begins May with an opening balance of $2,000 and employs 2 full-time florists.

The partnership has current assets of $12,400 and current liabilities of $7,900. Emma wants a refrigerated display cabinet costing $4,500 to cut flower wastage, but buying it now would use most of the remaining cash. The Hartleys are considering postponing the cabinet for three months, or switching office subscribers to weekly rather than monthly payment.

questions.question_text: Calculate the forecast closing balance for May. Show your working.
questions.model_answer: Closing balance for May = opening balance + net cash flow = $2,000 + ($8,700 - $10,300) = $2,000 - $1,600 = $400. [2]

knowledge_max_2: May net cash flow = $8,700 inflows - $10,300 outflows = -$1,600
Closing balance = $2,000 opening + (-$1,600) = $400

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the May closing balance is forecast to be so low.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: May outflows exceed inflows [k]; the forecast shows $10,300 of outflows against $8,700 of inflows, a net cash flow of -$1,600 [app]. Reason 2: wedding takings are uneven and do not cover the month [k]; although May includes $1,900 from two weddings, office subscriptions are billed monthly, so cash received cannot absorb the flower, wage and delivery costs before the month closes [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the Hartleys could improve the florist's cash flow in June.

Way 2: postponing the refrigerated cabinet purchase cuts outflows [k]; holding the $4,500 cabinet spend out of May, a deficit month, keeps cash in the partnership until June's forecast net cash flow of +$1,650 arrives [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Reducing the time taken to collect receivables speeds up cash inflows
Delaying or cancelling capital expenditure reduces cash outflows
application_max_2: Applies weekly vs monthly subscriptions to inflow timing and closing balance
Applies the $4,500 cabinet against May's -$1,600 net cash flow and June's +$1,650
analysis_max_2: Explains weekly billing accelerates cash without discounting
Explains delaying the cabinet avoids spending in the weakest month

questions.question_text: Do you think Emma and Lucy should buy the refrigerated display cabinet now, or postpone it for three months? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The Hartleys could argue for buying the cabinet now because it cuts wastage in a flower business where stock perishes quickly [k]. scenario_stem:

It repairs 30 yachts a year and stores 18 boats ashore each winter. Current assets are $61,000 including $19,000 owed by boat owners, and current liabilities are $44,000. December inflows are forecast at $7,600 against outflows of $13,900, and January at $5,400 against $9,700.

The yard begins December with an opening balance of $12,500. Rosa is considering a 20% winter service discount to fill idle slipways, and she plans a February bulk buy of $8,500 in paint and antifoul. She could instead delay the bulk buy to April, or press boat owners to settle the $19,000 they owe before offering any discount.

questions.question_text: Outline two ways the boatyard could overcome its winter cash shortfall.

scenario_stem:
Marigold Bakery & Patisserie is a private limited company founded 4 years ago in Country X by Samira Chaudhry, supplying 14 supermarkets with bread and celebration cakes. Its ovens run from 4 a.m. and supermarket invoices are paid 30 days late. Current assets are $52,000 and current liabilities are $29,000. March inflows are forecast at $41,200 against outflows of $46,700, and April at $48,900 against $43,300; the bakery begins March with an opening balance of $6,400.

Samira's two largest supermarket chains owe the bakery $23,500 between them. She is considering a 4% early-payment discount to bring the money in sooner, a $25,000 bank loan at 9% interest, and postponing the $11,000 mixer replacement by six months. She must decide before the March payroll is due.

questions.question_text: Define 'liquidity'.
questions.model_answer: Liquidity is the ability of a business to convert its assets into cash quickly and to meet its short-term debts as they fall due (current liabilities of $29,000 must be payable out of current assets of $52,000). [2]

knowledge_max_2: Liquidity is how quickly assets can be turned into cash
Liquidity measures the ability to pay short-term debts as they fall due

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to the bakery of offering the 4% early-payment discount.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: cash arrives sooner [k]; instead of waiting 30 days late, the bakery collects part of the $23,500 owed before the March payroll, lifting the March closing balance above the forecast $900 [app]. Benefit 2: the discount is cheaper than the alternative finance [k]; a 4% discount costs $940, while a $25,000 bank loan at 9% interest costs $2,250 a year, so the discount saves about $1,310 [app].

knowledge_max_2: An early-payment discount speeds up cash inflows from debtors
A small discount can cost less than interest on a loan
application_max_2: Applies $23,500 owed and the closing balance of only $900 vs the March payroll

questions.question_text: Explain two drawbacks of the 4% early-payment discount for the bakery.
questions.model_answer: Drawback 1: the discount directly reduces profit [k]; giving up $940 of margin on $23,500 assumes both chains take the discount and pay on time, and the bakery still needs cash for the March payroll [app][an]. Drawback 2: it may set a precedent [k]; if the two largest supermarket chains expect a 4% discount every month, the $940 loss repeats while the April recovery of +$5,600 net cash flow is no guarantee that future invoices come in quickly [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: An early-payment discount sacrifices profit to improve cash flow
Repeated discounts set a costly precedent with large customers
application_max_2: Applies $940 cost of the discount vs both chains taking it and the March payroll
Applies the repeat cost vs April's +$5,600 net cash flow forecast
analysis_max_2: Explains the saving is only real if chains accept and pay quickly
Explains repeated discounting compounds the margin loss

questions.question_text: Do you think Samira should offer the early-payment discount, or take the $25,000 bank loan? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Samira could argue for the early-payment discount because it fixes the root cause - slow-paying supermarkets [k]. At 4% it costs $940, far below the $2,250 annual interest on the $25,000 loan, and every pound collected early improves the March closing balance forecast at only $900 [app][an]. However, the discount works only if the chains agree and pay promptly, so uptake may be weak and a loan could still be needed to bridge the $5,500 March deficit [app][an]. Because the discount is cheaper and strengthens the customer relationship [k][eval], the evidence favours offering the 4% discount now while arranging a standby overdraft in case uptake is slow, keeping the $25,000 loan, and the $11,000 mixer postponement, as back-up options [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Early discounting targets the cause of the shortfall rather than its symptoms
A standby facility is a cheaper form of contingency than an unconditional loan

Applies the $5,500 March deficit and the $11,000 mixer postponement as fallback
analysis_max_2: Explains the discount is cheaper only if chains actually take it
Explains keeping the loan as back-up covers the risk of weak uptake
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation sequencing discount first, backup finance second
Weighs certain saving vs uncertain uptake in the supermarket chain context

scenario_stem:
Thornfield Freight is a private limited company operating 9 HGVs in Country X, delivering to supermarkets and builders' merchants across two provinces. January inflows are forecast at $34,600 against outflows of $39,800, while February inflows are $44,300 against outflows of $38,200. The business was founded 7 years ago and begins January with an opening balance of $8,900, with current assets of $74,000 and current liabilities of $41,000.

Thornfield owes its diesel supplier $28,000, due in late February. Customers owe the freight firm $41,000, of which $19,000 is more than 60 days overdue. Marcus Vale, the managing director, must decide whether to delay the diesel payment by 30 days, press customers to settle the overdue $19,000 first, and postpone the $16,000 tyre replacement to April.

questions.question_text: Calculate the working capital for Thornfield Freight. Show your working.
questions.model_answer: Working capital = current assets - current liabilities = $74,000 - $41,000 = $33,000. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Working capital = current assets - current liabilities
Working capital of $33,000 shows Thornfield's short-term resources exceed short-term debts

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons for the negative net cash flow forecast in January.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: January outflows exceed inflows [k]; the forecast shows $39,800 of outflows against $34,600 of inflows, a net cash flow of -$5,200 [app]. Reason 2: customers pay late and do not cover the gap [k]; customers owe $41,000, of which $19,000 is more than 60 days overdue, so January inflows barely reflect work already done [app].

knowledge_max_2: A net cash flow deficit occurs when outflows exceed inflows
Slow-paying debtors delay inflows even after work is done
application_max_2: Applies $34,600 inflows and $39,800 outflows = -$5,200 net cash flow
Applies $41,000 owed with $19,000 overdue over 60 days to the weak January inflows

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Thornfield could face if it delays the $28,000 diesel payment by 30 days.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: the supplier could refuse further deliveries [k]; delaying the $28,000 diesel payment by 30 days risks a stoppage, and without fuel the HGVs cannot complete the deliveries that generate February's $44,300 inflow [app][an]. Problem 2: postponement builds a larger bill [k]; the payment lands in February, when outflows already reach $38,200 against inflows of $44,300, so a late $28,000 payment on top could still strain the account despite the +$6,100 February net cash flow [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Delaying payments to suppliers risks refusal of future supplies
Postponing a payment does not remove the obligation, it just moves it
application_max_2: Applies the $28,000 diesel payment vs February's $44,300 inflow and the nine HGVs
Applies February outflows of $38,200 and the +$6,100 net cash flow to the extra $28,000
analysis_max_2: Explains a fuel cut-off would stop deliveries and revenue entirely
Explains February cannot absorb both its own bills and a deferred $28,000 comfortably

questions.question_text: Do you think Marcus should delay the diesel payment, or press customers to pay the overdue $19,000 first? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Marcus could argue for delaying the diesel payment because suppliers often accept 30 days more credit and fleet operations matter most [k]. But the diesel supplier can stop deliveries immediately, halting the nine HGVs and putting the $34,600 January workload at risk, whereas the $19,000 owed to Thornfield is legally due already [app][an]. Chasing the overdue debts first brings in cash without interest or reputational risk, and even partial collection would cover the January net cash flow of -$5,200 [app][an]. Because the overdue customer debts are the cheaper and more certain source of cash [k][eval], the evidence favours pressing customers to settle the $19,000 while negotiating a written 30-day extension with the diesel supplier in parallel and keeping the $16,000 tyre replacement for April [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Delaying supplier payment is a common but risky remedy for a cash shortage
Collecting overdue debts is the safest way to raise cash without borrowing
application_max_2: Applies the nine HGVs and $34,600 January workload to the fuel cut-off risk
Applies the $19,000 overdue vs the -$5,200 January net cash flow
analysis_max_2: Explains unilateral non-payment risks the fleet halting entirely
Explains collecting the $19,000 closes the gap without new debt
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation to chase debtors first with a parallel written supplier deal
Weighs supplier goodwill against debt collection certainty and cost

scenario_stem:
Fennick & Grey Foods Ltd is a private limited company in Country X that mills oats into breakfast cereal for supermarket chains. For the year ended 30 April 2026 the income statement showed Revenue of $486,000, Cost of Sales of $312,000, Gross Profit of $174,000, Expenses of $96,000 and Profit for the year of $78,000. A dividend of $30,000 was paid to shareholders, leaving a Retained Profit of $48,000.

The statement of financial position at 30 April 2026 shows non-current assets of $540,000, current assets of $210,000 and current liabilities of $90,000, giving working capital of $120,000 and capital employed of $660,000. Non-current liabilities are $160,000, so shareholders' equity is $500,000. Directors must decide between Option 1, a special dividend of $20,000, and Option 2, using the $48,000 retained profit towards a new dehuller costing $120,000.

questions.question_text: Define 'Revenue'.
questions.model_answer: Revenue is the total income a business earns from selling its goods or services during a trading period, before deducting any costs [2].

knowledge_max_2: Total income earned from selling goods and/or services
Earned during a trading period, before any costs are deducted

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why profit is important to Fennick & Grey Foods Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Profit can be retained and reinvested, funding growth such as the new dehuller without extra borrowing [k], and the $48,000 Retained Profit shows that such funds are genuinely available [app]. Reason 2: Profit rewards shareholders for their risk, enabling the $30,000 dividend paid this year [k], which helps maintain investor confidence in the $500,000 of equity [app].

knowledge_max_2: Profit can be retained and reinvested to fund growth without borrowing
Profit rewards owners/shareholders and enables dividends to be paid
application_max_2: $48,000 Retained Profit is available towards the dehuller
$30,000 dividend paid, rewarding shareholders in a company with $500,000 equity

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the income statement is useful to the directors when choosing between the special dividend and the dehuller.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The income statement confirms the company earned a Profit for the year of $78,000 after Expenses of $96,000, so the business is genuinely profitable and not just cash-rich [k], which tells directors that either option is genuinely affordable rather than a gamble on one good quarter [app][an]. Reason 2: It shows Retained Profit of $48,000 after the ordinary dividend of $30,000, indicating exactly how much could be committed towards the dehuller [k], so directors know Option 2 would use only two-fifths of the machine's cost and a further funding route would still be needed [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Confirms the business is profitable after deducting expenses
Shows retained profit available after dividends
application_max_2: $48,000 Retained Profit vs the dehuller's $120,000 cost
analysis_max_2: Sustainable profit means either option is affordable, not dependent on a windfall
$48,000 covers only two-fifths of the cost, so a further funding plan is required

questions.question_text: Do you think the directors should pay the $20,000 special dividend (Option 1) or use the retained profit towards the dehuller (Option 2)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option 1 rewards shareholders for their risk and signals confidence in the company, returning part of the profit directly to investors [k], and it would be affordable given current assets of $210,000 and working capital of $120,000 [app], which should keep shareholders loyal ahead of the expansion [an]. Option 2 keeps the $48,000 inside the business and directs it towards the dehuller, protecting the future Gross Profit base rather than distributing it once [k][app][an]. Overall, Option 2 is the stronger choice because the dehuller should improve milling efficiency and lift future profits for every shareholder, whereas the special dividend is a one-off reward that shrinks the funds available for growth; the directors can revisit a dividend next year once the machine's returns are proven [eval][eval].

knowledge_max_2: Dividends reward and retain shareholders
Retained profit can fund productive investment for long-term growth
application_max_2: Option 1 special dividend of $20,000 affordable from $210,000 current assets / $120,000 working capital
Option 2 keeps $48,000 retained towards the $120,000 dehuller
analysis_max_2: Dividend boosts loyalty now but leaves nothing for the machine
Dehuller should improve efficiency and protect/lift future Gross Profit
evaluation_max_2: For: immediate reward and signal of strength / option 2 costs shareholders cash
Against/Overall: Option 2 maximises long-term value; dividends can be paid once returns are proven

scenario_stem:
Fenwick Refrigeration Ltd is a private limited company in Country X that services refrigeration units for supermarket and restaurant chains. In the year ended 31 March 2026 it earned Revenue of $1,150,000, with Cost of Sales of $690,000, Gross Profit of $460,000, Expenses of $350,000 and Profit for the year of $110,000. The company paid an ordinary dividend of $40,000 and retained the remaining $70,000.

The statement of financial position at 31 March 2026 shows non-current assets of $820,000, current assets of $300,000 (including inventories of $95,000) and current liabilities of $130,000. Working capital is $170,000 and capital employed is $990,000. Non-current liabilities comprise a $300,000 long-term bank loan, so shareholders' equity is $690,000. The bank will waive $6,000 of interest if $100,000 is repaid early (Option 1), or the business could buy a new delivery van for $92,000 (Option 2).

questions.question_text: Define 'Current Assets'.
questions.model_answer: Current assets are assets a business expects to convert into cash, sell or use within one year, such as inventories, trade receivables and cash at bank [2].

knowledge_max_2: Assets expected to be sold, used or turned into cash within 12 months
Examples: inventories, trade receivables, cash at bank

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why positive working capital is important to Fenwick Refrigeration Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Working capital pays the day-to-day running costs such as engineers' wages and supplier invoices, and Fenwick's $170,000 of working capital keeps its service visits operating smoothly [k][app]. Reason 2: Working capital shows whether current assets exceed current liabilities, and with $300,000 against $130,000 the company can meet its short-term debts on time [k][app].

knowledge_max_2: Covers day-to-day operating outflows such as wages and supplier bills
Indicates ability to meet short-term debts as they fall due
application_max_2: $170,000 working capital funds the servicing operation

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the bank would study this statement of financial position before restructuring the loan.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The bank checks whether current assets can absorb an early $100,000 repayment, and with $300,000 available (including $95,000 of inventories) the cover looks adequate [k][app][an]. Reason 2: The bank assesses how the $300,000 long-term loan sits against the $990,000 capital employed and the $690,000 of shareholders' equity backing it, judging whether rescheduling keeps the loan secure [k][app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Bank assesses liquidity/capacity to absorb extra or early repayments
Bank checks solvency: loan size relative to capital employed and equity
application_max_2: $300,000 current assets including $95,000 inventories vs $100,000 repayment
analysis_max_2: After repayment, roughly $200,000 of current assets would remain, still ahead of $130,000 current liabilities
Equity of $690,000 gives the bank confidence restructuring adds no meaningful default risk

questions.question_text: Do you think Fenwick Refrigeration Ltd should repay $100,000 of the loan early (Option 1) or buy the delivery van (Option 2)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option 1 would cut non-current liabilities from $300,000 and save $6,000 of interest, improving the balance sheet the bank assesses and freeing future cash flow for debt service [k][app][an]. Option 2's van would let the company reach more supermarket and restaurant contracts, protecting the $1,150,000 Revenue base and the servicing margin it generates [k][app][an]. Overall, Option 2 is the better decision because the guaranteed $6,000 saving is modest beside the Revenue the van could win, and with $300,000 of current assets covering $130,000 of current liabilities a $92,000 purchase still leaves working capital positive; the loan can be rebalanced next year once retained profits have rebuilt equity [eval][eval].

knowledge_max_2: Early repayment cuts interest costs and improves the balance sheet
Investing in assets can generate additional revenue
application_max_2: Option 2 costs $92,000 and supports the $1,150,000 Revenue base
analysis_max_2: Lower debt improves future cash flow and bank relations
Van increases capacity to service more contracts; purchase still leaves working capital positive
evaluation_max_2: For Option 1: guaranteed $6,000 saving and lower risk / frees no new income
Overall: Option 2 wins on revenue generation; balance sheet remains healthy afterwards

scenario_stem:
Carrowmore Weavers Ltd is a private limited company in Country X weaving wool fabrics for made-to-measure tailoring businesses. In the year ended 31 January 2026 it recorded Revenue of $380,000, Cost of Sales of $228,000, Gross Profit of $152,000, Expenses of $87,000 and Profit for the year of $65,000. Despite this profit, the company held only $18,000 in its bank account.

Current assets total $208,000, including $120,000 owed by customers (one major customer settles around 60 days late) and inventories of $70,000. Current liabilities are $150,000, including $112,000 owed to suppliers, so working capital is $58,000. Non-current assets are valued at $410,000 and non-current liabilities at $150,000, giving capital employed of $468,000 and shareholders' equity of $318,000. Directors must choose between Option 1, an overdraft from the bank, and Option 2, asking suppliers to extend payment terms by 30 days.

questions.question_text: Outline the difference between profit and cash.
questions.model_answer: Profit is the surplus remaining after all costs are deducted from Revenue in the income statement, whereas cash is the money actually received and paid; a credit sale counts as profit before the cash arrives [2].

knowledge_max_2: Profit = Revenue minus all costs, as reported in the income statement
Cash = money actually received and paid; timing differences make the two diverge

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Carrowmore Weavers Ltd is profitable but short of cash.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Much of its earnings is tied up as $120,000 owed by customers, some of whom pay around 60 days late, so Revenue is recognised before the cash arrives [k][app]. Reason 2: The company must still pay Expenses of $87,000 and suppliers the $112,000 it owes, so cash goes out before the corresponding income is collected [k][app].

knowledge_max_2: Credit sales create profit before cash is received
Costs must be paid when incurred, regardless of when cash arrives
application_max_2: $120,000 owed by customers, one pays about 60 days late
$87,000 expenses and $112,000 owed to suppliers still must be paid

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the statement of financial position shows how Carrowmore Weavers Ltd could improve its cash position.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The $120,000 of receivables inside current assets could be collected faster with firmer payment terms, immediately lifting the $18,000 cash balance without any new finance [k][app][an]. Reason 2: Suppliers are owed $112,000, so Option 2's extra 30 days would defer cash outflow, protecting working capital of $58,000 while the receivables are collected [k][app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Convert receivables to cash faster through stronger credit control
Defer payments to suppliers by negotiation
application_max_2: $120,000 receivables vs only $18,000 in the bank
$112,000 owed to suppliers could be stretched 30 days under Option 2
analysis_max_2: Faster collection rebuilds the cash balance with no borrowing cost
Deferring outflow bridges the timing gap, keeping the business solvent month to month

questions.question_text: Do you think the directors should take the overdraft (Option 1) or ask suppliers to extend terms by 30 days (Option 2)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: An overdraft would cover the immediate gap and is simple to arrange, but it is repayable on demand and its interest would eat into the $65,000 profit [k][app][an]. Option 2 defers the $112,000 supplier outflow at no direct cost and suits a profitable company with $58,000 of working capital waiting on $120,000 of receivables [k][app][an]. Overall, Option 2 is preferable in the short term because Carrowmore is profitable and its problem is timing, not solvency; the directors should chase the $120,000 receivables firmly and keep the overdraft only as a backup if a major customer defaults [eval][eval].

knowledge_max_2: Overdrafts give immediate cash but are repayable on demand and carry interest
Extending supplier terms is cost-free short-term finance
application_max_2: Overdraft interest would reduce the $65,000 profit
Option 2 stretches the $112,000 supplier bill while awaiting $120,000 of receivables
analysis_max_2: Option 1 solves the gap quickly but increases financing cost and dependency
Option 2 aligns outflow with expected inflow, stabilising the $58,000 working capital
evaluation_max_2: For Option 1: certainty and immediacy / for Option 2: no cost but relies on supplier goodwill
Overall: Option 2, with the overdraft as backup — collect receivables and the cash crisis passes

scenario_stem:
Hollyhock Nurseries Ltd is a private limited company in Country X that grows ornamental plants and sells them to garden centres across the region. In the year ended 30 June 2026 it recorded Revenue of $240,000, Cost of Sales of $110,000, Gross Profit of $130,000, Expenses of $62,000 and Profit for the year of $68,000. A dividend of $25,000 is proposed, leaving Retained Profit of $43,000.

The statement of financial position shows non-current assets of $350,000, current assets of $160,000 (including cash of $55,000) and current liabilities of $70,000, giving working capital of $90,000 and capital employed of $440,000. Non-current liabilities are $120,000, so shareholders' equity is $320,000. To fund a $200,000 expansion the board is choosing between Option 1, issuing new shares to a small group of investors, and Option 2, expanding gradually from retained profits of about $43,000 a year.

questions.question_text: Define 'Shareholders' Equity'.
questions.model_answer: Shareholders' equity (shareholders' funds) is the owners' stake in the business, equal to capital employed minus non-current liabilities, made up of share capital plus retained profit and reserves [2].

knowledge_max_2: The owners'/shareholders' stake in the business
Equals share capital + retained profit, or capital employed − non-current liabilities

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why retained profit is an attractive way to fund the expansion.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Retained profit is finance the business already owns, so it does not have to be repaid — keeping non-current liabilities at $120,000 unchanged [k][app]. Reason 2: Using retained profit avoids issuing new shares, so existing shareholders keep their proportional control of the $320,000 of equity [k][app].

knowledge_max_2: Retained profit is permanent, internal finance — not repayable
Retained profit avoids diluting existing shareholders' control
application_max_2: Existing $320,000 equity remains in the same hands

questions.question_text: Explain two effects on shareholders' equity and on the expansion if Option 1 is chosen rather than Option 2.
questions.model_answer: Point 1: Issuing new shares for $200,000 would raise shareholders' equity immediately from $320,000 to $520,000, providing the whole expansion fund at once [k][app][an]. Point 2: Option 2 adds only about $43,000 to equity each year, so building a similar fund would take around five years of retained profits while the expansion waits [k][app][an].

knowledge_max_2: A new share issue increases share capital and equity by the amount raised
Retained profit builds equity gradually through reserves
application_max_2: Equity would jump from $320,000 to $520,000 under Option 1
$43,000 a year means around five years to approach $200,000 under Option 2
analysis_max_2: Option 1 lets the expansion proceed immediately and shares risk with new investors
Option 2 delays the project and keeps ownership unchanged, but growth is slow

questions.question_text: Do you think the board should issue new shares (Option 1) or expand gradually from retained profits (Option 2)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option 1 provides the full $200,000 immediately, letting Hollyhock respond to garden centre demand at once and lifting shareholders' equity to $520,000 without adding interest-bearing debt [k][app][an]. Option 2 avoids dilution and keeps every decision with the current owners, but at $43,000 a year the company would need roughly five years to match the fund, risking lost seasonal sales [k][app][an]. Overall, Option 1 is justified because Profit of $68,000 and Retained Profit of $43,000 prove trading strength, but not enough speed to seize the opportunity; new investors would enlarge the equity that backs the expansion and share the risk, so long as dividend expectations are negotiated carefully to protect existing owners [eval][eval].

knowledge_max_2: New share issues raise finance quickly and share risk with investors
Retained profit is the cheapest internal finance and preserves control
application_max_2: Option 2 yields about $43,000 a year — around five years to build a similar fund
analysis_max_2: Option 1 enables immediate expansion and faster growth in Revenue
Option 2 preserves control but loses the timing advantage of the opportunity
evaluation_max_2: Against Option 1: dilution and dividend expectations may pressure profits
Overall: Option 1, since retained profits alone are too slow to fund a time-sensitive expansion

scenario_stem:
Redhall Textiles Ltd is a private limited company in Country X weaving upholstery fabric for furniture manufacturers. In the year ended 31 August 2025 Revenue was $500,000, Cost of Sales $300,000, Gross Profit $200,000, Expenses $120,000 and Profit for the year $80,000. In the year ended 31 August 2026 Revenue rose to $650,000, but Cost of Sales jumped to $455,000, leaving Gross Profit of $195,000 and, after Expenses of $140,000, Profit for the year of only $55,000.

The directors are deciding between Option 1, raising the average selling price by 8% from September 2026, and Option 2, switching to a cheaper yarn supplier who would cut Cost of Sales by 10% but may reduce fabric quality. questions.question_text: Define 'return on capital employed' (ROCE).
questions.model_answer: Return on capital employed measures the percentage return a business earns on the capital invested in its operations, calculated as profit divided by capital employed multiplied by 100; Pellham Bay Hotel earned $570,000 divided by $3.8 million multiplied by 100 = 15.0% this year, down from 20.0% last year ($400,000 divided by $2.0 million). [2]

knowledge_max_2: ROCE = profit / capital employed x 100

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the managing director should worry about the falling ROCE before Phase 2.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: ROCE shows the return the hotel earns on each dollar of capital employed [k]; it fell from 20% last year ($400,000 divided by $2.0 million) to 15% ($570,000 divided by $3.8 million), even though profit rose, showing the borrowed $1.8 million wing is not yet earning its keep [app]. Reason 2: ROCE lets the director benchmark the hotel against the industry average of 14% [k]; at 15% Pellham barely beats that benchmark, so adding a further $1.5 million in Phase 2 without higher occupancy risks ROCE slipping below the industry average [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of using ROCE to judge the new wing's performance.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: ROCE uses balance-sheet figures and historic carrying values, not what the wing could be worth now [k]; if property values have risen above the $3.8 million carrying value, the 15% ROCE understates the wing's true return [app][an]. Limitation 2: ROCE ignores non-financial measures that explain performance [k]; occupancy of only 62% and the cost of servicing the borrowed money do not appear in the ratio, so Phase 2 must also weigh occupancy trends and borrowing risk [app][an].
